subject: diving beetle larva
title: This 2-Inch Larva Stabs Tadpoles and Drinks Them Through Its Jaws

scenes.text: In this pond, something two inches long is drinking the tadpoles.
The water tiger, the larva of a predaceous diving beetle. It hangs motionless among the weeds, jaws wide open, waiting.
A tadpole swims past. It strikes and clamps on with hollow, sickle-shaped jaws.
Through those jaws it pumps brown digestive juice into its prey. That kills it and melts it from the inside. Then the larva sucks the juices back out.
It takes small fish, snails, leeches and other water tigers, prey bigger than itself, and breathes through snorkel holes on its tail.
Then it crawls ashore, pupates in the mud, and returns as a beetle. Hard shell, air bubble under its wings, and still hunting tadpoles.

description:
The larva of a predaceous diving beetle, called a water tiger, grabs tadpoles and small fish with hollow sickle-shaped jaws, injects digestive juice and sucks out the liquefied prey.
Water tigers can reach about 2 inches long. They hang still among pond weeds, strike prey that swims past, inject enzymes through channels in their pincers, and feed on prey larger than themselves, including small fish, tadpoles, snails, leeches and other water tigers. They breathe through spiracles at the tail tip, raised to the surface like a snorkel. Mature larvae crawl ashore to pupate; the adult beetles trap an air bubble under their wing covers to dive, and eat fish, tadpoles and frogs. The family Dytiscidae has about 4,300 species worldwide.
What's the scariest thing you've found in a pond?
first_comment: Hollow jaws, digestive juice in, liquid tadpole out. What is the most brutal pond creature you know?
